entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15265" type="x-p"/> All the men that willingly offered - Some volunteered their services, which was considered a sacrifice to patriotism at that time, as Jerusalem afforded very few advantages, and was a place of considerable danger; hence the people spoke well of them, and no doubt prayed for God's blessing upon them.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15266" type="x-p"/> Now these are the chief - A good deal of difference will be found between the enumeration here and that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.2">1Chr 9:2</reference>, etc. There, those only who came with Zerubbabel appear to be numbered; here, those, and the persons who came with Ezra and Nehemiah, enter into the account.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen15269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15270" type="x-p"/> And Shabbethai - This verse, with <reference osisRef="Neh.11.20">Neh 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.21">Neh 11:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.28">Neh 11:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.29">Neh 11:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.32">Neh 11:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.33">Neh 11:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.34">Neh 11:34</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Neh.11.35">Neh 11:35</reference>, are all wanting in the Septuagint and the whole chapter is wanting in the Arabic, the translator not being concerned in Jewish genealogies. <div eID="gen15270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15271" type="x-p"/> The outward business - Calmet supposes that he provided the victuals for the priests, victims for the sacrifices, the sacerdotal vestments, the sacred vessels, and other necessaries for the service of the temple.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen15273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15274" type="x-p"/> It was the king's commandment - By the king some understand David, and others Artaxerxes. It is most probable that it was the latter; who wished that a provision should be made for these, a part of whose office was to offer up prayers also, as well as praises. For we know that Darius made an ample provision for the priests, that they might offer sacrifices of sweet savor unto the God of heaven; and pray for the life of the king and of his sons, <reference osisRef="Ezr.6.10">Ezr 6:10</reference>. Some have thought that they had been Jewish singers employed in the service of the Persian king, to whom he had given a salary, and to whom he wished still to continue the same.
